newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar grapples with long-term economic plans, emir.
newsitem.headline: Qatar grapples with long-term economic plans, emir.

text.p: Qatar is still grappling with the problems of long-term economic planning for an economy which depends on the fluctuating price of oil, the Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani said on Monday.
He also told the country's consultative Shura council in a speech that the Gulf Arab state would press ahead with moves towards more liberalisation and public participation in government.

"The main problem facing us...is the need to provide the necessary financial resources to cover public spending and big production projects implemented by the government, especially in the oil, gas and infrastructure fields in the midst of difficult economic and financial circumstances...due to low oil prices," he said.

"Despite the recent improvement in prices, the long-term effects of this problem remain the same, especially that the improvement in prices is not steady...but is usually followed by a decrease in prices and continued fluctuation which makes it difficult to lay down fixed long-term planning," he added.
Qatar, an Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) member, receives about 70 percent of its state revenue from oil sales and the rest from hydrocarbon-based industries.

Its oil reserves are exceeded by natural gas deposits, which are the world's third largest after Russia and Iran. It is due to start exporting liquefied natural gas in December, which economists expect to boost its economy.
Qatar has said it plans to balance its budget by the year 2000. Its 1996-97 budget projected a reduced deficit of 2.95 billion riyals ($810 million) from the 1995-96 deficit of 3.53 billion.

"We were successful last year...in dealing with the existing circumstances by several measures including cutting down on spending and controlling it and alleviating the burdens on the government system," the emir said.
He said a public role in government was vital.

The emir, who ousted his father Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad al-Thani last year, has issued draft laws for municipal and chamber of commerce board elections for the first time in Qatar. He has also increased the number of members in the consultative Shura council to 35 from 30.
The emir said Qatar would soon have a new, permanent constitution, replacing one in force since 1971.

"We think it's time to draw up a (new) permanent constitution that takes into account the progress which has taken place...in the last quarter of a century, to deepen our pioneering experience in popular participation...to increase its role in drawing and executing state policies", he said. ($1=3.64 riyals)
